sections.label: Updating Court oath practice
sections.summary: The speaker proposes updating Singapore's Court oath practice to align with other common law jurisdictions and reflect multi-religious values.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: As we continue to strengthen our status as a regional and global legal hub, I propose we update our Court practice of taking oaths in Singapore when giving evidence, to bring this in line with the practice in other major common law jurisdictions and better reflect our nation's multi-religious values and expectations of witnesses who give evidence in our Courts.

sections.label: Oaths for all faiths
sections.summary: The speaker proposes allowing persons of all faiths to take oaths per their beliefs when giving evidence, deposing affidavits or making statutory declarations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Based on current Court practice and the Act, only persons of the Christian faith are allowed to take oaths when giving evidence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This provision was, however, repealed when the current Act was enacted in 2000 on the basis the repealed provision was largely historical and intended to cater to our largely migrant society in the past where different communities carried with them different customs on how oaths were to be made.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I propose that the current practice in Courts and under the Act be updated so as to allow persons of all faiths to take oaths in accordance with their religious beliefs when giving evidence in Courts, deposing affidavits or making statutory declarations.

sections.label: Affirmation as alternative
sections.summary: Those with other beliefs or conscientious objections can make an affirmation, which under the Oaths and Declarations Act has the same legal effect as an oath.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: But the important point is that this practice does not affect those with other religious beliefs or those who conscientiously object to the taking of an oath.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: This is because they can avail themselves of another established alternative − making an affirmation.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: Under the Oaths and Declarations Act, the taking of an oath has the same legal effect as making an affirmation.

sections.label: Maintaining current oath system
sections.summary: The speaker says there is no need to change, as administering oaths for all religions would be difficult and costly, and affirmation already suffices.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: First, there is no need to do so, given that an affirmation has the same legal effect as an oath and is neutral.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: There are many religions in the world today − some are well-established, others less so.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: It would be difficult to expect us, or the Courts, to have sufficient knowledge about all religions so as to be in a position to administer oaths correctly under each of those religions.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: This will come at a considerable cost and does not seem necessary in light of the fact that the existing practice allows for persons of all religious beliefs to take an affirmation, which has the same legal effect as an oath.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: It is, therefore, best for us to maintain our current system, which has worked well for us for many years.
